_note: Stowage factor is the volume one tonne of cargo occupies, in cubic metres per tonne. It decides whether a vessel WEIGHS OUT (hits its deadweight or draft limit with hold space to spare) or CUBES OUT (fills its holds before reaching deadweight). Dense cargo such as iron ore weighs out. Light cargo such as thermal coal cubes out. Every value here is a typical published mid range figure and is marked as an assumption until the team verifies it against a stowage factor table or an actual bill of lading.
_handling_note: handling_rate_multiplier scales the port discharge rate and the origin load rate. Dense free flowing ores move faster per tonne through a grab than coal does. Scrap is markedly slower because it is handled with magnets and orange peel grabs and does not flow.

cargo_types.name: Coking coal
cargo_types.notes: Metallurgical coal for the blast furnace. The reference cargo for this system.

citations.stowage_factor_m3_per_t: ASSUMPTION - typical published range 1.15 to 1.30 m3/t. Verify against a stowage factor table.
citations.handling_rate_multiplier: ASSUMPTION - defined as the 1.0 reference case.

cargo_types.name: Thermal coal
cargo_types.notes: Steam coal. Lighter and bulkier than coking coal, so it cubes out sooner.

citations.stowage_factor_m3_per_t: ASSUMPTION - typical published range 1.25 to 1.40 m3/t. Verify against a stowage factor table.
citations.handling_rate_multiplier: ASSUMPTION - assumed equal to coking coal.

cargo_types.name: Iron ore
cargo_types.notes: Very dense. Always weighs out, filling well under half the hold volume. This is why ore trades are draft driven rather than volume driven.

citations.stowage_factor_m3_per_t: ASSUMPTION - typical published range 0.35 to 0.45 m3/t. Verify against a stowage factor table.
citations.handling_rate_multiplier: ASSUMPTION - dense free flowing cargo moves more tonnes per grab cycle.

cargo_types.name: Manganese ore
cargo_types.notes: Ferroalloy feed. Dense, weighs out like iron ore.

citations.stowage_factor_m3_per_t: ASSUMPTION - typical published range 0.40 to 0.55 m3/t. Verify against a stowage factor table.
citations.handling_rate_multiplier: ASSUMPTION - assumed slightly below iron ore.

cargo_types.name: Limestone
cargo_types.notes: Flux for the blast furnace. Moderately dense, normally weighs out.

citations.stowage_factor_m3_per_t: ASSUMPTION - typical published range 0.70 to 0.90 m3/t. Verify against a stowage factor table.

cargo_types.name: Steel scrap
cargo_types.notes: Grade dependent to an unusual degree. Baled or bundled scrap stows near 0.6 m3/t while loose HMS can exceed 1.3 m3/t. Slow to handle because it does not flow.

citations.stowage_factor_m3_per_t: ASSUMPTION - wide published range 0.6 to 1.4 m3/t depending on grade and baling. HIGH UNCERTAINTY. Verify per fixture.
citations.handling_rate_multiplier: ASSUMPTION - scrap is handled with magnets and grabs and is materially slower than bulk.
